CsRecordPatternOpen filters record-pattern sites by the receiver's judged
type. Open — TRecordOpen — means lowering has no full sorted field set
and takes offsets from the pattern's own index. The read composes two
existing homes: graph_chase resolves the receiver handle through the
union-find, so a TVar needs no separate walk, and fold_strip is types.mn's
own alias, refinement and repr-pin peel.

The build's most useful output is a kill. The first draft filtered only
let bindings, marched, and answered 0 for the wheel — which read as
confirmation that the previous pin's annotations had worked. Falsification
refused that reading: removing one annotation left the count at 0. Both of
the wheel's record-pattern sites are match arms, not let bindings, so the
shape was blind to exactly what it was built to count and its zero meant
nothing. The comment justifying the omission was wrong too, since
MatchExpr carries the scrutinee node. That is the second toothless gate
this session caught by falsifying rather than by review.

Corrected, the shape is discriminating both ways: 0 with both receivers
annotated, 1 with backends/wasm:1100 located when one is removed.
record_pattern_open_max: 0 holds it, and zero is a contract rather than a
tolerance — a complete pattern over an open row is structurally identical
to a partial one, so no discipline at the site distinguishes safe from
unsafe and only this count can.

Banked, not asserted: fold_sig maps TRecord and TRecordOpen to the same
signature, so an open and a closed record with the same known fields share
generated helpers. Whether that is wrong is unmeasured —
Hbeta.fold.open-record-shares-closed-signature carries the probe.

clob/59ed8e6:
The first real Bet 7 test overturns the preview, and the pre-registration
gets honored rather than reinterpreted.

A small dense core (d=64) trained on Moby-Dick, nine checkpoints, each
measured on the held-out split for both capability (clob eval-dense) and
lambda1 (clob regime --dense). lambda1 climbs once -- random init to the
first checkpoint (-0.35 -> -0.11, horizon 2.9 -> 9.0 tokens) -- then
drifts BACK toward deep contraction as capability keeps improving. The
best-capability checkpoint sits at lambda1 -0.28, horizon 3.6 tokens; the
best checkpoints have the SHORTEST memory. Spearman rho(lambda1,
capability) = -0.27 over all points, -0.81 over trained checkpoints: a
strong NEGATIVE relation. The core earns its gains by forgetting harder,
not by nearing the edge of chaos.

Literal verdict against the pre-registered thresholds: INDETERMINATE (rho
never reaches +0.6 to pass; |rho| not below 0.2 and best lambda1 not below
-1 to kill). But the finding is not ambiguous -- the positive-tracking
hypothesis is falsified. The kill clause has a gap: a strong negative rho
falsifies the near-critical thesis as hard as no correlation does, so a
corrected Bet 7 should kill on rho <= -0.2 too. Per the discipline that
fix belongs in a separate commit, not this reporting of the run -- flagged
in the notes, not applied here.

This is the branch ATTRACTOR.md's Bet 7 prose named: selective-state
architectures partly earn their keep by forgetting on purpose. Part III's
'capability => edge of chaos' reading is challenged by its own instrument;
ATTRACTOR.md now says so at the point it makes the claim and at Bet 7.
Caveat kept honest: one architecture, one corpus, <1 epoch, and next-token
BPE over prose is a largely local task -- the thesis may be corpus-
dependent rather than simply wrong. The earlier 3-point preview saw only
the initial climb and read it as confirmation; the full test corrects it.

perennials/59b207b:
Found by clicking a link the harness had just built: SearchProvider read
the URL once at mount and then treated it as write-only, so any in-app
navigation that carried params — a bed's Open in the guide, a gap link
from the almanac, the Back button crossing search states — landed on
stale constraints, and the write-back effect then wiped the very params
the link had carried. Full page loads worked, which is why it survived
every earlier check.

One effect now owns both directions. lastWritten tells the cases apart:
an incoming string this provider wrote is her own edit echoing back; an
incoming string it never wrote is someone else's navigation, and state
adopts it. Her edits still ride replace, so constraint changes spam no
history.
